title: Process Scheduling

key_ideas: Scheduling Criteria (Throughput, Turnaround, Waiting, Response Time)
Scheduling Algorithms (FCFS, SJF, Round Robin, Priority)
prerequisites: Concept of a Process and Process Control Block (PCB)

misconceptions: Believing preemptive scheduling permanently terminates a running process when it is interrupted.
Assuming Shortest Job First (SJF) is straightforward to implement in real-world general-purpose operating systems without estimation.
Thinking a smaller time quantum in Round Robin scheduling always improves system throughput.
Confusing the role of the CPU scheduler (selecting a process) with the role of the dispatcher (executing the context switch).
Believing priority scheduling naturally prevents process starvation without explicit mechanisms like aging.

rubric.text: Explains that process scheduling is the operating system function that selects which runnable process in memory gets access to the CPU.
Differentiates preemptive scheduling (where the OS can interrupt a running process) from non-preemptive scheduling (where a process runs until it yields, blocks, or terminates).
Defines key scheduling performance metrics including CPU utilization, throughput, turnaround time, waiting time, and response time.
Explains First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) scheduling and describes how the convoy effect occurs when short processes wait behind a long CPU-bound process.
Explains Shortest Job First (SJF) and Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) scheduling, noting why they minimize average waiting time and why exact burst times are difficult to predict.
Explains Round Robin (RR) scheduling, including how the size of the time quantum impacts performance and context-switching overhead.
Describes Priority Scheduling, the issue of starvation for low-priority processes, and how aging solves starvation by gradually increasing a process's priority over time.
Explains Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ) scheduling and how it dynamically adjusts process priority based on historical behavior (such as CPU vs I/O bound behavior).
